chunks.source_name: Peter Attia MD
chunks.summary: VO2 max is the single strongest predictor of all-cause mortality and longevity. Moving from 'low' to 'below average' VO2 max reduces mortality risk more than quitting smoking. Maintaining or improving VO2 max through high-intensity interval training (e.g., Norwegian 4×4) is the highest ROI longevity intervention for already-fit individuals.
chunks.canonical_claim: VO2 max is the strongest independent predictor of all-cause mortality. Actively training VO2 max via HIIT/4x4 intervals is a top-tier longevity intervention.

chunks.source_name: Meta-analysis: Concurrent Training Interference
chunks.summary: Concurrent training (strength + cardio in same program) produces an 'interference effect' — cardio can blunt hypertrophy and strength gains. Effect is largest when cardio is high-volume, high-intensity, and performed before lifting. Mitigated by: separating sessions by 6+ hours, keeping cardio moderate in volume, prioritizing lower-intensity cardio (Zone 2), and ensuring adequate recovery/nutrition.
chunks.canonical_claim: Interference effect from concurrent training is real but manageable. Separate sessions by 6+ hours, use low-moderate cardio intensity/volume relative to lifting, and optimize recovery.

chunks.source_name: ISSN Position Stand
chunks.summary: Optimal protein intake for muscle hypertrophy and retention in resistance-trained athletes is 1.6–2.2g/kg/day. Higher intakes (up to 3.1g/kg lean mass) show no harm and may be beneficial during caloric restriction. Spread over 3–4 meals for maximal muscle protein synthesis. 40g+ per meal may be better for older athletes (>40) due to anabolic resistance.
chunks.canonical_claim: 1.6–2.2g/kg/day protein for hypertrophy; older athletes may benefit from 40g+ per meal and higher overall intake due to anabolic resistance.

chunks.source_name: BJSM / Weekly Volume Meta-analysis
chunks.summary: Dose-response relationship between weekly volume and hypertrophy: 10–20 sets per muscle group per week is the practical effective range for intermediate-advanced athletes. Beyond 20+ hard sets may induce junk volume or excessive fatigue. DJN's volume (4 sets chest, 4 back, 2 shoulders, 2 arms, 2–3 legs) sums to ~14–15 working sets/session which is within optimal range.
chunks.canonical_claim: 10–20 hard sets per muscle group per week is the evidence-based sweet spot; DJN's 14–15 sets per full-body session is optimal.

chunks.source_name: JAMA Network Open
chunks.summary: Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is inversely and independently associated with all-cause and cardiovascular mortality. Every 1-MET increase in CRF reduces all-cause mortality by ~13%. Elite vs. low-fit individuals have 5× lower mortality risk. No upper limit of benefit has been identified for moderate-high CRF gains.
chunks.canonical_claim: Higher cardiorespiratory fitness = dramatically lower mortality risk. Improving VO2 max and CRF is the highest-return longevity intervention available.

chunks.source_name: British Journal of Sports Medicine
chunks.summary: Muscle-strengthening activities are associated with a 10–17% reduction in all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and diabetes, independent of aerobic exercise. Benefits plateau around 30–60 min/week of resistance training. The combination of aerobic + resistance training is additive for mortality reduction.
chunks.canonical_claim: Resistance training 30–60 min/week reduces all-cause mortality by 10–17%; combining with aerobic exercise provides additive benefits.

chunks.source_name: European Journal of Applied Physiology
chunks.summary: Functional overreaching (short-term overtraining) causes temporary performance decline that reverses in days. Non-functional overreaching takes weeks to months to resolve. True overtraining syndrome is rare in individual-sport athletes but presents as: persistent performance decline, mood disturbance, suppressed HRV, sleep disruption, low libido, and elevated resting HR. Libido decline is an early warning sign.
chunks.canonical_claim: Suppressed libido, persistent low HRV, sleep disruption, and declining strength across 2+ sessions are early overtraining markers requiring immediate load reduction.

chunks.source_name: Applied Sciences
chunks.summary: Heart rate variability (HRV) is a reliable, non-invasive marker of autonomic nervous system recovery and readiness. Suppressed HRV (below 7-day rolling average) indicates incomplete recovery, elevated sympathetic tone, or early overtraining. HRV-guided training (reduce intensity when HRV is low) outperforms fixed periodization in several studies.
chunks.canonical_claim: HRV below 7-day rolling average is a valid signal to reduce training intensity or volume. HRV-guided training improves outcomes versus fixed plans.

chunks.source_name: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
chunks.summary: Creatine monohydrate is the most well-researched sports supplement. It increases muscle phosphocreatine stores, improves high-intensity exercise capacity, and augments training adaptations. 3–5g/day is effective for maintenance. Higher doses (10–20g/day) show no additional benefit for most athletes but are safe.
chunks.canonical_claim: Creatine 3–5g/day is sufficient for maintenance and performance enhancement; loading phases are optional and not superior long-term. Higher doses up to 20g/day are safe.

chunks.source_name: Norwegian University of Science and Technology
chunks.summary: The Norwegian 4×4 protocol (4 min at 85–95% HRmax, 3 min active recovery × 4 rounds) is one of the most effective methods to improve VO2 max. Shown to improve VO2 max by 7–10% over 8 weeks in trained individuals. Max once per week for trained athletes to allow full recovery.
chunks.canonical_claim: Norwegian 4×4 is highly effective for VO2 max improvement; once per week maximum for trained athletes due to recovery demands.

chunks.source_name: ISSN
chunks.summary: Caffeine is one of the best-evidenced performance enhancers. 3–6mg/kg bodyweight taken 30–60 min pre-exercise improves endurance, strength, power output, and reduces perceived exertion. 3 flat whites (≈240mg caffeine) falls in the effective range for DJN (80kg → 240–480mg optimal). Habitual use reduces acute effect but performance benefit persists.
chunks.canonical_claim: Caffeine 3–6mg/kg (~240–480mg for 80kg athlete) 30–60 min pre-workout is evidence-backed for strength and endurance performance.

chunks.source_name: DJN Athlete Profile
chunks.summary: DJN: 43yo male, 181cm, ~80kg, ~8–11% body fat, 25–27 years training age. Goals: longevity, cardiovascular fitness, maintain muscle mass. Full-body lifting every other day. Cardio on off days: VO2 max running (1–2x/week), Norwegian 4×4 (max 1x/week), Zone 2 (~1x/week). Nutrition: 2800–3200 kcal, 200–230g protein, 270–320g carbs, 70–90g fat. First meal noon (IF). Post-workout eating delay ~2.5h.
chunks.canonical_claim: DJN trains full-body every other day, prioritizes VO2 max and longevity, eats intermittent fasting with first meal at noon. 200–230g daily protein target.

chunks.source_name: DJN Supplement Stack
chunks.summary: DJN daily supplements: Omega-3 (360mg EPA/240mg DHA), Magnesium glycinate 150mg, Glycine 2g, NAD+ 1000mg, Ashwagandha 2400mg, Urolithin A 2000mg, Vitamin D3+K2 2000IU, Zinc bisglycinate 225mg, Boron 4mg, Creatine 10–15g, Glutamine 5g, Whey 50g, Clear whey 40g, Casein 50g. Every-other-day: Methylene blue 10ml, Cumin oil 2–3mg.
chunks.canonical_claim: DJN's complete supplement stack with daily and alternate-day protocols as specified.

chunks.source_name: DJN Rule Engine
chunks.summary: DJN recovery-gated training rules: High recovery → proceed as planned, high intensity allowed. Moderate recovery → reduce volume ~15%, no failure sets, consider Zone 2 over VO2. Low recovery → -30% volume, no failure sets, block high-intensity cardio. If 2+ high-intensity cardio done this week → next must be Zone 2. Norwegian 4×4 max once per week. If strength declines 2 consecutive sessions AND high cardio load → reduce VO2 frequency.
chunks.canonical_claim: DJN's training decisions are gated by recovery state (high/moderate/low) with specific volume and intensity adjustments per state.

chunks.source_name: Layne Norton / BioLayne
chunks.summary: Creatine is especially valuable for athletes over 35. It helps maintain muscle mass, supports cognitive function, and may have longevity benefits. Taking 10–15g/day (as DJN does) saturates stores quickly without loading and is a reasonable high-dose approach.
chunks.canonical_claim: Creatine is strongly beneficial for older athletes; 10–15g/day is a high-dose but safe approach that maximizes muscle saturation.

chunks.source_name: Peter Attia MD
chunks.summary: Zone 2 training (roughly 60–70% of max HR, conversational pace) is the foundation of aerobic base building. It improves mitochondrial density, fat oxidation efficiency, and metabolic flexibility. Attia recommends 3–4 hours/week minimum for longevity. Zone 2 should make up 80% of total cardio volume with Zone 5 (VO2 max work) making up ~20%.
chunks.canonical_claim: Zone 2 makes up 80% of optimal cardio prescription for longevity; 3–4h/week minimum. Pairs with ~20% high-intensity (Zone 5) for VO2 max gains.

chunks.source_name: Menno Henselmans
chunks.summary: The 'anabolic window' is real but longer than the old 30-minute myth. Muscle protein synthesis remains elevated for 3–5 hours post-exercise. For fasted morning trainers with a 2.5h post-workout eating delay, muscle protein synthesis is still actively stimulated by the workout and protein intake within that window is effective.
chunks.canonical_claim: Post-workout anabolic window is 3–5 hours, not 30 minutes. A 2.5h eating delay post-training is still effective for muscle protein synthesis.

chunks.source_name: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
chunks.summary: Ashwagandha (KSM-66) at 300–600mg/day reduces cortisol, improves stress response, and has shown modest but statistically significant improvements in testosterone in men. At 2400mg/day (DJN's dose), it is a high dose; studies use 300–600mg KSM-66. Recovery and sleep quality improvements are well-documented.
chunks.canonical_claim: Ashwagandha 300–600mg/day (KSM-66) is evidence-backed for cortisol reduction, sleep quality, and modest testosterone support. DJN's 2400mg dose is higher than studied doses.

chunks.source_name: Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research
chunks.summary: Omega-3 (EPA+DHA) supplementation reduces exercise-induced muscle soreness, attenuates inflammation, and may support muscle protein synthesis, especially in older athletes. 2–4g EPA+DHA per day is recommended for athletes. DJN's dose of 360mg EPA/240mg DHA (600mg total) is below the optimal therapeutic range of 2–4g.
chunks.canonical_claim: Omega-3 2–4g EPA+DHA/day reduces inflammation and soreness; DJN's current 600mg dose is likely subtherapeutic for maximum anti-inflammatory effect.

chunks.source_name: Sleep Medicine
chunks.summary: Glycine 3g before bed improves subjective sleep quality, reduces time to sleep onset, and decreases daytime sleepiness. Mechanism involves lowering core body temperature. DJN's 2g dose is slightly below studied dose of 3g but still likely effective.
chunks.canonical_claim: Glycine 3g before bed improves sleep quality and reduces sleepiness. 2g is slightly below the evidence-based dose but still beneficial.

chunks.source_name: Menno Henselmans
chunks.summary: Training to failure is not required for hypertrophy and increases systemic fatigue substantially. Stopping 1–3 reps from failure (RIR 1–3) produces equal or better results with less accumulated fatigue. For advanced athletes maintaining intensity, training to failure occasionally is acceptable but should not be the default, especially during high cardio weeks.
chunks.canonical_claim: Training to failure occasionally is fine; RIR 1–3 is the optimal default for long-term hypertrophy with lower fatigue accumulation.

chunks.source_name: Journal of Nutrition
chunks.summary: Casein protein before bed (40g) increases overnight muscle protein synthesis and reduces whole-body protein breakdown. Particularly beneficial when training occurred in the same day. The slow-digesting nature of casein sustains amino acid availability for 5–7 hours during sleep.
chunks.canonical_claim: 40g casein before bed is evidence-based for overnight muscle protein synthesis; particularly effective on training days.

chunks.source_name: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology
chunks.summary: Vitamin D3 deficiency is associated with lower testosterone, impaired muscle function, and increased inflammatory markers. 2000–5000 IU/day is commonly recommended for athletes. K2 (MK-7 form) directs calcium to bones rather than arteries. Optimal serum 25(OH)D is 40–60 ng/mL.
chunks.canonical_claim: Vitamin D3 2000–5000 IU/day with K2 supports testosterone, muscle function, and reduces inflammation. Aim for serum 40–60 ng/mL.

chunks.source_name: Menno Henselmans
chunks.summary: Protein distribution across meals matters for muscle protein synthesis. 40–50g high-quality protein per meal (especially for athletes over 40) maximizes MPS due to anabolic resistance. With a compressed eating window (noon to 9pm), hitting 200–230g protein requires larger protein portions per meal — this is achievable with DJN's food choices (quark, whey, casein, meat).
chunks.canonical_claim: For athletes 40+, 40–50g protein per meal in 3–4 meals maximizes MPS. Compressed IF windows require large protein portions per meal.

chunks.source_name: Jeff Nippard
chunks.summary: Fasted training does not meaningfully impair muscle retention when total daily protein is adequate (1.6–2.2g/kg). Performance may be slightly reduced in truly fasted states but the effect is small for trained athletes. If training fasted or semi-fasted, prioritize post-workout protein intake within 2 hours.
chunks.canonical_claim: Fasted training is compatible with muscle retention when daily protein targets are met (1.6–2.2g/kg). Post-workout protein timing becomes more critical in fasted training.

chunks.source_name: Nature Metabolism
chunks.summary: Urolithin A is a mitophagy activator derived from pomegranate/gut bacteria. Clinical trials (Timeline Longevity) show it improves mitochondrial health markers, muscle endurance (+12% in older adults), and reduces inflammatory markers. 500–2000mg/day studied. Limited data in highly trained athletes.
chunks.canonical_claim: Urolithin A (500–2000mg/day) activates mitophagy and improves muscle endurance in sedentary to lightly active older adults. Limited evidence in high-level athletes.

chunks.source_name: Huberman Lab
chunks.summary: Magnesium glycinate taken 30–60 min before bed improves sleep quality by activating GABA receptors. Huberman recommends 200–400mg magnesium glycinate before bed. DJN's 150mg dose is on the lower end but still effective, especially combined with glycine.
chunks.canonical_claim: Magnesium glycinate 200–400mg before bed improves sleep quality via GABA activation; 150mg still beneficial.

chunks.source_name: Jeff Nippard
chunks.summary: Body recomposition (building muscle while losing fat simultaneously) is most achievable in: beginners, detrained individuals, or intermediate/advanced athletes in a small caloric surplus at maintenance. At 8–11% body fat with 25+ years training, meaningful recomposition is very slow but possible. DJN's best strategy is maintenance or very slight surplus, high protein, creatine, and consistent periodization.
chunks.canonical_claim: Body recomposition at advanced training age and low body fat is slow but possible at maintenance calories with high protein and consistent training.

chunks.source_name: Huberman Lab
chunks.summary: HRV is best measured first thing in the morning before getting out of bed using a consistent protocol. Consistent low HRV over multiple days warrants a forced deload or rest. Acute low HRV (single day) may just reflect alcohol, poor sleep, or high-stress the day before and not require changing the training plan.
chunks.canonical_claim: Single-day HRV dip may be noise; multiple consecutive low-HRV days are the real signal to reduce load.

chunks.source_name: Jeff Nippard
chunks.summary: Full-body training 3× per week stimulates each muscle group 3× at moderate volume per session. For advanced athletes training every other day (~3–4x/week), full-body is well-matched: each muscle group gets stimulated frequently enough for hypertrophy, and volume per session is manageable. Frequency of 2–3x/week per muscle group is optimal.
chunks.canonical_claim: Full-body every-other-day training achieves optimal stimulus frequency (2–3x/week per muscle) for hypertrophy in advanced athletes.

chunks.source_name: Huberman Lab
chunks.summary: Time-restricted eating with a first meal at noon (~8–10h fasting window) aligns with circadian biology and supports metabolic health. Huberman recommends avoiding eating for 1 hour after waking to allow cortisol peak to do its job. Some studies show IF improves insulin sensitivity and metabolic markers even without caloric restriction.
chunks.canonical_claim: Noon first meal / IF aligns with circadian cortisol rhythm and supports metabolic health. Delaying first meal 1+ hour after waking is evidence-consistent.

chunks.source_name: Nutrition
chunks.summary: Zinc supplementation raises testosterone in zinc-deficient individuals. If zinc status is already normal, additional supplementation does not meaningfully raise testosterone. Athletes frequently deplete zinc through sweat. Zinc bisglycinate is well-absorbed form. 25–40mg elemental zinc per day is typically studied.
chunks.canonical_claim: Zinc supplementation raises testosterone only in deficient individuals; athletes are at higher risk of zinc depletion. Zinc bisglycinate is optimal form.

chunks.source_name: Menno Henselmans
chunks.summary: Deloads every 4–8 weeks (reduce volume 40–50%, keep intensity) are evidence-based for clearing accumulated fatigue and supercompensation. Reactive deloads (triggered by performance declines, HRV suppression, or motivational crash) are as effective as scheduled deloads. Two consecutive sessions of strength decline warrants investigating recovery status.
chunks.canonical_claim: Deload every 4–8 weeks or reactively when performance drops 2+ consecutive sessions. Cut volume 40–50%, maintain intensity.

chunks.source_name: Biological Trace Element Research
chunks.summary: Boron supplementation (3–10mg/day) may increase free testosterone and decrease SHBG in some studies. Evidence is limited and largely observational. DJN's 4mg/day dose is within the studied range. Likely beneficial as an adjunct to a comprehensive supplement protocol.
chunks.canonical_claim: Boron 3–10mg/day may modestly increase free testosterone by reducing SHBG. Evidence is preliminary but dose is safe.

chunks.source_name: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
chunks.summary: Glutamine supplementation shows limited benefit for muscle recovery or hypertrophy in well-nourished athletes. Primary benefits are gut barrier integrity, immune support, and reducing muscle soreness. 5g/day is a typical dose. More beneficial during periods of very high training volume or caloric restriction.
chunks.canonical_claim: Glutamine 5g/day supports gut health and immune function but has minimal direct hypertrophy or recovery benefit in well-fed athletes.
